prompt: A consumer writes its checkpoint and then does the work. It crashes between the two. What happens to that record?

choices.text: It is processed twice
choices.why: That is the other order: work first, then checkpoint.

choices.text: It is lost: the restart begins after it
choices.why: Right: at most once. Nothing is done twice, and this record is never processed.

choices.text: Kinesis notices the crash and redelivers it
choices.why: Kinesis knows nothing of the consumer; it serves whatever iterator it is asked for.

choices.text: It is processed exactly once
choices.why: No ordering of the two steps gives that; the work never happened.

prompt: Why is "exactly once" not a third way of ordering the work and the checkpoint?
hint: The two writes go to different systems.

choices.text: Because the checkpoint is always written first
choices.why: It can be written in either order; that is what the two guarantees are.

choices.text: Because it needs a faster network
choices.why: Speed makes the window smaller and never closes it.

choices.text: Because Kinesis forbids it in its terms of use
choices.why: It is a matter of two separate writes, not of a rule.

choices.text: No single write covers the two
choices.why: Right: a crash between them either loses or repeats. Exactly once is built from atomic writes or idempotent work, end to end.

prompt: Why is at-least-once the default of Kinesis, Firehose, Lambda and Kafka?
hint: Which of the two can be repaired afterwards?

choices.text: It is the only one that loses nothing
choices.why: Right: duplicates can be handled afterwards, lost records cannot. At most once fits only data that may be lost.

choices.text: It is cheaper to run than at most once
choices.why: Both cost the same to run; they differ in what a crash does.

choices.text: It removes duplicates on its own
choices.why: It creates them; removing them is the consumer's job.

prompt: A producer's retry put `o-301` into the shard twice, at sequence numbers 1 and 2. Why can the sequence number not identify the copy?

choices.text: Sequence numbers are reused after a retry
choices.why: They were 1 and 2: different, never reused.

choices.text: Each copy got a number of its own
choices.why: Right, so only a key in the data can show they are one payment: the order id, put there by the producer.

choices.text: moto's sequence numbers are small integers
choices.why: On AWS they are long strings, and the copy still gets a new one.

choices.text: The sequence number is encrypted
choices.why: It is a plain position in the shard.

prompt: A team builds an idempotency key from customer id, amount and date. What goes wrong?
hint: Can two real events share all three?

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the date includes the time zone
choices.why: The fault is not the date's precision; the key describes the event instead of naming it.

choices.text: The key is too long for DynamoDB
choices.why: A few dozen characters is well within a key's size.

choices.text: Two real orders become one
choices.why: Right: two orders of the same amount that day share the key, and a payment is lost. The key has to be an id assigned once when the event happens, like the order id.

choices.text: A producer's retry is no longer caught
choices.why: A retry has the same three values, so it would be caught; the error runs the other way.

prompt: Which of these can put the same record into a consumer's hands twice? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four places were named, and one thing that looks like a duplicate and is not.

choices.text: A producer that retries after a lost acknowledgement
choices.why: Right; the shard holds both copies.

choices.text: A consumer that crashes before its checkpoint
choices.why: Right; the restart reads the batch again.

choices.text: A worker losing its lease to another during a rebalance
choices.why: Right; the new owner starts from the last checkpoint.

choices.text: Two customers paying the same amount on the same day
choices.why: Those are two real events, not a duplicate.

prompt: In `plain` mode, after the crash and the restart, `c-17` showed 20,340 cents instead of 12,780. Why did the restart read the first four records again?

choices.text: No checkpoint had been written, so it started at `TRIM_HORIZON`
choices.why: Right. The checkpoint is written once, at the end, and the crash came first.

choices.text: moto resent the records after the crash
choices.why: moto served the iterator it was asked for; the consumer asked for the beginning.

choices.text: DynamoDB rolled back the four updates
choices.why: Nothing was rolled back; that is why the totals doubled.

choices.text: `ADD` reads every record twice
choices.why: `ADD` applies once per call; the calls were repeated.

prompt: Why does `totals.py` put the dedupe `Put` and the `ADD` in one transaction instead of two writes one after the other?
hint: Imagine a crash between the two separate writes.

choices.text: A transaction is cheaper than two writes
choices.why: It costs twice an ordinary write per item; it is paid for correctness.

choices.text: DynamoDB accepts `attribute_not_exists` only inside a transaction
choices.why: A plain `put-item` takes the condition too, as the lab's first test of it showed.

choices.text: A transaction makes the writes run in parallel
choices.why: The point is that they succeed or fail together, not their speed.

choices.text: So that a crash cannot record an order without counting it
choices.why: Right, nor count one without recording it. Either both writes happen or neither does.

prompt: With the dedupe on, the whole stream of seven records was replayed. How many items did `quitanda-processed` hold afterwards?
hint: One per payment, not per record.

prompt: The table of processed order ids grows by one item per payment for ever. What bounds it, and at what price?
hint: DynamoDB can delete items when they expire.

choices.text: A time to live past the longest replay
choices.why: Right, and duplicates older than it are no longer caught. The window is chosen on purpose, from the stream's retention plus a margin.

choices.text: Deleting the table every night; nothing is lost
choices.why: A replay the next morning would then count every order again.

choices.text: Nothing bounds it, and nothing needs to
choices.why: It costs storage per item for ever; a TTL ends that.

prompt: A consumer writes each batch to S3 under a key named after the time of writing. It crashes after the write and before the checkpoint, and replays. What is in the lake?
hint: Compare the two listings of the section.

choices.text: One object, because S3 overwrites the old one
choices.why: An overwrite needs the same key; the time made a new one.

choices.text: Two objects with the same records, and every query counts both
choices.why: Right. A key from the shard and sequence range would have landed on the same object.

choices.text: No object, because S3 refuses identical bytes
choices.why: S3 compares nothing; it stores what it is given under the key given.

choices.text: Two objects, and S3 marks the second as a duplicate
choices.why: S3 has no such mark.

prompt: In the lab, `ADD 500` twice made 1,000 and `put-item` of 500 twice left 500. When can a consumer use the second?
hint: An upsert carries the whole state.

choices.text: Whenever the table has a sort key
choices.why: The key schema has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: When the records arrive in order
choices.why: Order matters to which snapshot wins, not to whether the write repeats safely.

choices.text: When each event carries the new state
choices.why: Right: a balance, not an amount to add. A stream of changes, like payments, still needs the dedupe.

choices.text: Never with DynamoDB, only with SQL's `MERGE`
choices.why: `put-item` is exactly an upsert; the lab ran it.

prompt: A write is ___ when repeating it leaves the same result as doing it once.
hint: The word the lesson's title ends on.

prompt: A consumer stores the highest sequence number it has applied, per shard, and skips anything at or below it. Which duplicates does that catch?
hint: What sequence number does a producer's retry get?

choices.text: Every duplicate, from any source
choices.why: A producer's retry arrives with a higher number and passes the test.

choices.text: Only the producer's retries
choices.why: The opposite: those get new, higher numbers.

choices.text: The consumer's replays
choices.why: Right: they come back with the same numbers. It is the checkpoint moved into the sink, one number per shard.

choices.text: None, because sequence numbers are not ordered
choices.why: Within a shard they increase, which is what makes the watermark work.

prompt: What does Kafka's idempotent producer, on by default since Kafka 3.0, remove?
hint: It works at the broker, per partition, within one producer session.

choices.text: Duplicates written by its own retries within one session
choices.why: Right. The broker recognises a number it already wrote and does not write it again.

choices.text: Duplicates a consumer creates by replaying
choices.why: A replay is the consumer reading again; the producer is not involved.

choices.text: Records with the same key
choices.why: That is compaction, and it keeps the latest per key; idempotence is about retries.

choices.text: Writes repeated into DynamoDB downstream
choices.why: Nothing in Kafka reaches past Kafka.

prompt: A Kafka consumer uses transactions and reads with `read_committed`, and writes each result to DynamoDB. Is the DynamoDB write exactly once?

choices.text: Yes, transactions cover every write the consumer makes
choices.why: They cover Kafka records and offsets; DynamoDB is outside.

choices.text: Yes, because `read_committed` hides duplicates
choices.why: It hides uncommitted transactions from readers, not repeated external writes.

choices.text: No: it is outside the transaction
choices.why: Right, so it has to be idempotent on its own. Exactly once is end to end, and this end is DynamoDB.

prompt: Match each source of duplicates to what catches it.
hint: One remedy works only inside Kafka.

pairs.right: An idempotency key in the data
The idempotent producer, at the broker

pairs.left: A consumer's replay of one shard

pairs.right: A dedupe when the lake is compacted

prompt: Put in order what `totals.py` in `dedupe` mode does with one record.
hint: The checkpoint is the last thing, and only once per run.
items: Read the record from the shard
Parse its order id, customer and amount
Try the transaction: put the order id if absent, and add the amount
If the transaction is cancelled, report a duplicate and move on
At the end of the shard, write the checkpoint

prompt: Quitanda's app sends "customer `c-17`'s loyalty points are now 340" after every order. Which sink design is simplest and correct under at-least-once delivery?
hint: Is the event a state or a change?

choices.text: A dedupe table of event ids in a transaction with an `ADD`
choices.why: It works, and it pays for a memory the event does not need: the event is a state.

choices.text: An `ADD` of 340 to the customer's points
choices.why: That adds a state as if it were a change, and counts it again on every replay.

choices.text: A `put-item` that sets the points to 340, with a version so an older event cannot overwrite a newer one
choices.why: Right. The upsert absorbs duplicates, and the version handles the order.

choices.text: Exactly-once delivery from Kinesis
choices.why: Kinesis offers at least once; there is no setting for exactly once.
